summary: Gives advice for protocol designers who use HTTP as a base for other application protocols, covering default ports, URL schemes, and security mechanisms. It is a Best Current Practice. It was replaced by RFC 9205.

plainLanguage.summary: Many new programs borrow the web's way of talking instead of inventing their own. This is a checklist of good manners for doing it well. It has been replaced by RFC 9205.

questions: should a new protocol be built on http
best practice for http based protocols
should a new protocol use http
should i reuse port 80 for my protocol
subtitle: Advice on when and how to build a new protocol on top of HTTP, from ports and URLs to status codes.

tldr.problem: Many designers wanted to layer new application protocols on HTTP, raising questions about ports, URL schemes, methods, media types and security.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC weighs HTTP's costs and benefits, then recommends: pick a new port for substantially new services, avoid reusing the http: scheme, describe proxy handling, and use only generic status codes.
tldr.outcome: This Best Current Practice (BCP 56) has been obsoleted by RFC 9205.

today: RFC 3205 is a Best Current Practice that has been obsoleted by RFC 9205, so read that document for current guidance.

sections.title: Why People Build on HTTP
sections.content:
The RFC lists reasons for the interest in using HTTP as a substrate: familiarity, compatibility with deployed browsers, reuse of servers and client libraries, easy prototyping with CGI scripts, existing security mechanisms, the ability to traverse firewalls, and cases where a server must support HTTP anyway.

Protocol reuse has a long tradition, such as Telnet under FTP and SMTP. The questions are whether to use a different port than 80, traditional or new methods, http: URLs or a new prefix, and existing or new MIME types.

It is advice, not a strict rule set, so the RFC 2119 key words are not used.
sections.plainLanguage: People like using the web's language for new things because everyone already knows it and lots of tools already speak it.

sections.title: Should You Use HTTP at All?
sections.content:
Complexity: HTTP grew persistent connections, byte ranges, content negotiation and caching. A layered protocol must support or circumvent them, and specifying a profile might cost more than designing a purpose-built protocol.

Overhead: HTTP plus TCP connection setup can be a poor choice if payloads are likely to stay under a few hundred bytes, so a UDP-based protocol should be considered. The setup cost can become negligible with HTTP/1.1 persistent connections when the same pair does several transactions.

Firewalls and NATs: getting through them is a common reason to pick HTTP, but if a firewall blocks unknown protocols, that is presumably a conscious policy. Attempting to circumvent it is not an acceptable justification.

The section ends with questions to ask, such as whether payload size is worth the overhead and whether the server must support HTTP anyway.
sections.plainLanguage: Ask yourself if you really need a big toolbox for a small job, and do not sneak past a locked gate just because you can.

sections.title: The Limits of HTTP Security
sections.content:
HTTP digest authentication and TLS are not enough alone for many applications. Digest needs a shared secret and offers no way to send it securely. A server compromise can expose many secrets.

TLS was designed to authenticate servers to clients. Browsers ship with certificate authority keys wired in, which works for a small number of servers but not for millions of clients, so client authentication is rarely used with TLS. A common pattern is TLS for the server plus a username and password over HTTP basic or digest.

For privacy, 40-bit ciphersuites are unsuitable, and even 56-bit DES has been broken in days. The RFC says neither TLS nor digest is a "magic pixie dust" solution, and designers must analyze their users' needs. TLS and SASL also work without HTTP.
sections.plainLanguage: A lock on the web's door does not automatically protect everything inside. You still have to think about who needs a key.

sections.title: Ports, URL Schemes and Media Types
sections.content:
Port 80: IANA reserved TCP port 80 for HTTP. A substantially new service should not usurp it. A new port is warranted if the service references different data, needs separate code, or its traffic must be easy to distinguish for firewalls. Otherwise it may be an extension, which should define new methods. New methods alone do not remove the need for a new port or URL type.

URL scheme: consider whether the scheme will be widely used, needs a new default port, needs different setup, or lets user interfaces improve usability. Appending an "s" to mean TLS is nonstandard and of limited value, so authentication details belong in URL parameters.

Media types: a MIME type describes the object, not the operation to apply. Choose existing frameworks such as text/directory or XML with care, minimize differences between HTTP and email encodings, and note that MIME email requires CRLF line endings for text/* while HTTP traditionally uses LF only.
sections.plainLanguage: A new service should get its own door number and its own sign rather than squatting in the web's room.

sections.title: Reusing Code and Status Codes
sections.content:
Existing HTTP libraries may have "http" assumptions wired in, so a client may convert xyz://host/something to an http form only when calling the library, and never expose that to users. A layered protocol must decide whether to send HTTP/1.1 in exchanges, and each one must specify how HTTP is used, including proxy interaction.

HTTP status codes are unlikely to express the specifics of other applications. At most, generic 200 (complete success) and 500 (complete failure) should signal errors from the message body, with detail in the body. Proxies and caches act on these codes, so the specification must prevent harmful caching of responses. Layered applications should not define new status codes. An application that cannot work with caching or altering intermediaries should not use HTTP as a substrate.
sections.plainLanguage: Do not invent new traffic-light colors. Stick to plain green and red, and put the details in a note.

sections.title: Summary of Recommendations
sections.content:
The RFC condenses its advice into five points: provide adequate security and analyze it, since HTTP or TLS alone does not suffice; do not circumvent firewall policies, and give substantially new services their own ports; in general do not reuse http: or other URL schemes; describe exactly how HTTP is used, including proxies; and follow the status code guidelines.

It is a Best Current Practice (BCP 56) written by Keith Moore.
sections.plainLanguage: Be secure, ask before sneaking through gates, use your own name tag, explain how you use the web, and keep error signals simple.

items.title: Security
items.text: HTTP or TLS alone does not give adequate security.

items.title: Ports
items.text: Do not circumvent firewalls; new services get new ports.

items.title: URL schemes
items.text: In general do not reuse http: or other schemes.

items.title: Describe HTTP use
items.text: Say how HTTP and proxies are used.
